attribution: Author unknown; presented as a dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess, and traditionally said to belong to the Rudrayamala Tantra
period: Scholars generally place it between roughly the 7th and 9th centuries CE; dates are uncertain
summary: A Shaiva contemplative text in which Bhairava answers the Goddess with a long series of meditative methods (dharanas), widely counted as 112.
whyRead: It is one of the most practice-centred texts of the Shaiva Tantras. Its methods use breath, sensation, emotion, sound, space and ordinary moments as doorways into awareness, grounded in a non-dual view of consciousness.
story: The Goddess asks Bhairava about the true nature of reality and of Bhairava himself. He answers that it cannot be captured in doctrine and instead teaches a series of contemplative practices through which it can be realised.
questions: Can ordinary experience become a doorway to awareness?
What is the nature of the ultimate reality, Bhairava?

keyTeachings.title: Beyond doctrinal description
keyTeachings.text: The frame dialogue sets aside ritual and conceptual accounts of the divine as preparatory, pointing instead to direct experience.

keyTeachings.title: A range of contemplations
keyTeachings.text: The methods, widely counted as 112, include attention to the pause between breaths, to sound as it fades, to open space, to intense emotion and to moments of wonder.

keyTeachings.title: Contemplation within a non-dual frame
keyTeachings.text: The practices assume that consciousness and its power (shakti) are one, so any experience, rightly attended to, can reveal its source.

keyTeachings.title: Within a ritual tradition
keyTeachings.text: Although it downplays external worship, the text belongs to the Bhairava Tantras and their ritual and theological world; later Kashmiri authors such as Kshemaraja commented on it.

structure.label: About 160 verses in the common text
structure.note: Frame dialogue, then the dharanas; the count of 112 is traditional and depends on how methods are grouped
